confidence_rationale: The normative-inference justification for MECH-456's rebinding rule: online Bayesian inference over an unbounded number of latent causes infers a NEW cause when the current one stops explaining the data, reproducing renewal/latent-inhibition and other context-dependent conditioning results. This is exactly 'drop the currently-bound configuration when a competitor better explains the situation', at the level of principle. Held below 0.75 because the timescale (across-trial conditioning contexts) and domain (associative learning) differ from MECH-456's within-episode perceptual binding, and the paper is a model of behavioural data rather than a neural or architectural test.
failure_signatures: Latent-cause inference here operates over conditioning CONTEXTS across trials (renewal, latent inhibition) -- a slower, associative-learning timescale than MECH-456's within-episode rebinding of a perceptual self<->world-config binding.

It is a normative Bayesian model fit to behavioural phenomena, not a neural or architectural mechanism; the 'switch to a new cause' is inferential, and the paper's own twist is that this capacity is LIMITED (absent in young animals / after hippocampal lesion), which MECH-456 does not model.

'A competitor overtakes' in MECH-456 is a comparison between concurrently-available configurations; latent-cause inference is more naturally 'the current cause stops fitting, infer a (possibly new) one' -- adjacent but not identical framings.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Context-dependent learning and extinction are modelled as normative statistical inference: online Bayesian inference within a model that assumes an unbounded number of latent causes categorises observations into causes and infers a NEW latent cause when existing ones stop explaining the data. This reproduces renewal and latent-inhibition results, and predicts that context dependence is reduced when the capacity to infer new causes is restricted (young animals, pre-training hippocampal lesions).
mapping.ree_translation: This is the normative principle underneath MECH-456's rebinding rule. The claim's biological grounding explicitly cites latent-cause inference (Gershman 2010/2017): 'switch causes when the current one stops explaining the data.' MECH-456 asserts the binder re-binds to a competing world-configuration when that competitor becomes the better explanation of the agent's realised situation. Gershman/Blei/Niv give the rational-inference form of exactly this move -- infer/switch to a different latent cause when the current one loses explanatory support -- and ground it as the optimal thing to do, not merely a mechanistic quirk. It supplies the 'why re-binding is the correct behaviour' half that the trigger papers (mechanism) and the object-file paper (updatability) do not.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The timescale and domain differ: latent-cause inference here spans conditioning contexts across many trials (renewal, latent inhibition), whereas MECH-456 rebinds within an episode over perceptual bindings. And 'competitor overtake' (comparing concurrent configurations) is subtly different from 'current cause stops fitting, infer a new one'. This is a principle-level grounding of the switch RULE, not a measurement of any binder; the paper's own emphasis on LIMITED new-cause capacity is not part of the claim.
mapping.source_context: Computational (normative Bayesian) model of animal associative-learning phenomena -- renewal and latent inhibition -- fit to behavioural data across developmental and lesion manipulations.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality high (Psychological Review, canonical latent-cause paper). Mapping fidelity moderate-good (0.66): the normative 'infer a new cause when the current stops explaining' is nearly MECH-456's rebinding rule, at the principle level. Transfer risk moderate (0.4): across-trial conditioning contexts vs within-episode perceptual binding; normative model of behaviour, not a neural/architectural test.
